analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay equal wages for jobs of equivalent skill, effort, and responsibility.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and received no vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Pay Act of 2007 would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to bar employers from paying lower wages to workers in jobs dominated by women or people of color when those jobs are equivalent in skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions to jobs held by higher-paid men or white workers. It also protected workers who discussed wages, added compensatory and punitive damages and class actions as remedies, and required employers above a size threshold to report pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it died without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and workers of color in female- or minority-dominated occupations who are paid less than workers in different but equivalent jobs — jobs requiring the same composite of skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions. Workers who fear retaliation for comparing pay also gain protection, since the bill bars employers from firing or intimidating anyone who inquires about, discloses, or discusses wages [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in female- and minority-dominated jobs

how_it_helps.text: Requires equal pay for 'equivalent jobs' — jobs that may be dissimilar but whose requirements are equivalent as a composite of skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions — going beyond the existing equal-work standard, which only covers the same or nearly identical jobs [S2, S3].

Prohibits employers from firing, coercing, or intimidating employees who ask about, disclose, or discuss their own or coworkers' wages, and prohibits retaliation against anyone who challenges a discriminatory wage practice [S3].

Allows courts to award compensatory and punitive damages, lets prevailing plaintiffs recover expert witness fees, and permits suits to proceed as class actions, making it practical for low-wage workers to bring claims [S2, S3].

Requires employers above a size threshold (25 or more employees at first, 15 or more thereafter) to file annual reports with the EEOC disclosing wage rates by job classification along with the sex, race, and national origin of employees at each rate, giving regulators and researchers pay-gap data they otherwise lack [S3].
Applies the same pay-equity standard to congressional and executive branch employees through conforming amendments to the Congressional Accountability Act and related law [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay below-market wages in female- or minority-dominated occupations would have to raise those wages. All covered employers would bear recordkeeping duties documenting how they set wages, annual pay-equity reporting to the EEOC, and increased exposure to class-action litigation and damages [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers with pay gaps across equivalent jobs

drawbacks.text: Determining whether two dissimilar jobs are truly 'equivalent' is inherently judgment-heavy, and courts would have to compare pay across occupations; employers and courts would likely face substantial litigation over job valuation [S3].

The bill shifts the burden to employers to prove that any pay differential rests on a job-related factor, and even a demonstrated business justification can fail if an employee shows a cheaper alternative practice existed — a demanding standard for businesses with many legitimate pay variables [S3].

Annual wage reporting by sex, race, and national origin imposes new compliance costs on employers with as few as 15 employees in later years, a burden smaller businesses acknowledged would fall hardest on them [S3].

Punitive damages and broad class actions could expose employers to outsized penalties for pay structures built up over years before the bill's effective date, which takes effect only one year after enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would raise pay for workers whose occupations are systematically underpaid because of who holds them — a real and measurable gain, backed by the bill's own findings citing the 76-cent female-to-male earnings ratio. The costs are real too: compliance paperwork, litigation over job comparisons, and higher wage bills for employers. The employer defenses preserved (seniority, merit, production systems, and bona fide job-related factors) keep the bill from freezing legitimate pay differences, but the equivalent-jobs standard still requires courts to make difficult cross-occupation value judgments, and the litigation and reporting burdens are significant.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then in July 2007 sent to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Representative Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2007 on April 24, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1, S5].
Ten House members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill [S4].
On July 9, 2007, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or Senate companion action is recorded; the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with pay differentials between equivalent jobs kept the status quo: no equivalent-jobs pay standard, no annual wage reporting by race and sex, and no expanded damages or class-action exposure. Workers in underpaid female- and minority-dominated occupations gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoided a new pay-equity standard

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired majority that set its agenda
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on July 9, 2007, and never brought it to a markup or vote; the subcommittee took no recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held. The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored, so whatever support existed was entirely from one party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force equal pay across equivalent jobs, require annual wage reporting by sex, race, and national origin, and expose employers to punitive damages and class actions. For businesses that profit from lower pay in female- or minority-dominated occupations, those costs come directly out of the wage gap the bill targets.

Small employers are exempt from the annual wage-reporting requirement below a size threshold (25 employees initially, 15 thereafter), easing compliance costs, but the equal-pay mandate and litigation exposure would apply to them just the same.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' employment bar and litigation services
industries.note: Class actions, expert fees for prevailing plaintiffs, and compensatory and punitive damages would expand the market for pay-discrimination suits. More litigation capacity runs alongside workers' ability to enforce the new right.
